newsitem.title: FRANCE: U.S. to act if EU rocks wheat price, official says.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to act if EU rocks wheat price, official says.

text.p: The United States is ready to think about bringing back export subsidies for its wheat if recently revived European Union subsidies rock the world market, a senior U.S. agriculture official said on Sunday.
In particular, any move by the EU to step up competition by sharply undercutting U.S. prices would be seen as "aggressive," Agriculture Department Under-Secretary Gene Moos told Reuters.
"We would certainly review it at that point," Moos said, asked whether Washington would bring out subsidies if the EU started competing with cheaper wheat from Argentina.
The EU, criticised by the U.S. for last month's decision to renew subsidies, has so far stuck to a pledge not to undercut the price of key U.S. soft red winter wheat on the world market.
But European grain exporters have been pressing for bigger EU subsidies to close a price gap with even cheaper Argentine wheat, which they say drives out business to North Africa.
"We would consider that fairly aggressive," Moos said in response to these calls for a decoupling with U.S. prices.

Traders said last week Argentine wheat from the harvest due in December was being offered for less than $145 per tonne. That compared with $160 for U.S. soft red winter and $175 for French wheat, which with EU export aid is sold for about $10 less.

One of the few big exporters without a much higher crop this year, Washington has so far resisted the temptation to restore its subsidised Export Enhancement Program (EEP) for wheat. It suspended the program last year when the EU also paused its subsidies as low grain stocks sent prices spiralling.
The EU has started using subsidies again to help farmers market what could be a record crop for the 15-nation bloc this year. But it has vowed not to be an aggressive seller.
Moos, in Paris for an international food fair, said he would meet French officials to talk about the crop and other issues.
He said he was concerned about the toll competition was already having on wheat prices. They have dived to their present levels from a record close to $300 per tonne early this year.
Big crops in Argentina and Australia have fuelled the selling, though without restoring stocks to previous levels.
"Given the direction of the market today, and also given that Argentina has been selling aggressively, we are concerned about the level to which prices can be driven down," he said.
He declined to say how far this might be, but warned prices could dip below the levels guaranteed to farmers inside the EU.
Brussels analysts say this would create a costly storage headache for the EU, which acts as buyer of last resort and is anxious not to return to unwanted "grain mountains" of the past.
"World stocks are still tight and we hope that most or all exporters will be able to market their share of wheat in a way that does not invoke subsidies," Moos said.
His remarks echo previous U.S. warnings about the danger of a subsidy spat.
Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman has threatened to fight subsidies with subsidies if necessary to preserve market share.

Trade adviser Paul Drazek, recently back in Washington from Brussels where he urged a subsidy freeze, told Reuters on Friday the EU export refunds were unnecessary. The EU should cut its own domestic prices to avoid having to use them, he said.
